Expo sixty-seven in Montreal celebrated Canada's centennial year as a young nation and established the fair as a spectacular showcase of architecture, design, and human culture on an unprecedented scale. It was officially opened on the centennial of Canadian Confederation, marking exactly a hundred years since the dominion's founding in eighteen sixty-seven. The fair positioned itself as a celebration of Canada's distinct identity and maturity as a nation coming into its own on the world stage. It was held on man-made islands in the Saint Lawrence River, specifically Île Sainte-Hélène and Île Notre-Dame, locations that showcased ambitious engineering and environmental transformation of remarkable proportions. Over fifty million visitors came from around the world to experience Expo sixty-seven. The fair featured Buckminster Fuller's Geodesic Dome, the American Pavilion, a striking sixty-meter hemisphere that symbolised technological innovation and became an enduring icon of the era and of futuristic architecture. The central theme was "Man and His World," which positioned the fair around human creativity and potential. Pavilions from sixty-two nations celebrated human creativity and diversity, presenting the achievements and cultures of the world's peoples. The fair introduced innovative transport systems, including a suspended Minirail and Minicab network, representing futuristic mobility concepts that visitors could actually ride and experience. It marked a pinnacle of world's fair design and cultural prestige, influencing exposition aesthetics and themes globally for decades to come.
